short_answer: Best not: fresh and dried apple can upset a chinchilla's gut. Give a dried, untreated apple wood stick instead.
No: the PDSA says bananas are best avoided because they are high in sugar and can upset a chinchilla's tummy. Banana chips are no better.
No: blueberries are sugary, wet fruit that can upset a chinchilla's gut. Dried raspberry or blackberry leaves are a safe berry-themed treat.
Best not: the PDSA says carrots are likely to upset a chinchilla's tummy. Dried herbs and a rose hip make safer treats.
Best not: celery is watery and stringy, which can loosen a chinchilla's droppings. Dried nettle, plantain or dandelion are safer greens.
Best not: cucumber is almost all water, which can loosen a chinchilla's droppings. Fresh water in a bottle and dried herbs are better.
Yes, dried: a couple of dried dandelion leaves or one flower head a few times a week. Fresh dandelion is wetter and best kept tiny or skipped.
No: the PDSA says grapes are high in sugar and best avoided, as they can upset a chinchilla's tummy.
Yes: unlimited grass hay such as timothy, meadow or orchard grass should be most of a chinchilla's diet, refreshed every day.
No: Burgess lists lettuce among foods to avoid for chinchillas, and its water can loosen droppings. Dried herbs and leaves are the safe greens.
No: VCA says never feed nuts and the RSPCA says avoid them, as they are high in fat. Hazel twigs are fine; the nuts are not.
We'd say no: the PDSA allows up to two raisins a week for adults, but VCA, PetMD and Chewy say no dried fruit. A dried rose hip is safer.
Yes, as a treat: one dried rose hip, once or twice a week at most. Dried rose petals and wild rose twigs are safe too.
No: strawberries are sweet, wet fruit that can upset a chinchilla's gut. Dried raspberry or blackberry leaf is a safer treat.
No: VCA says never feed seeds and the RSPCA says they are too high in fat. Sunflower seeds are among the fattiest of all.
Yes, rarely: one thumbnail-sized piece of apple with the pips removed, about once a month. Never for diabetic degus.
No. Banana is too sugary for degus, which are prone to diabetes. Choose leafy veg or a rare sliver of apple instead.
Yes: one small raw broccoli floret or leaf per degu, once or twice a week, mixed with other veg. Too much can cause wind.
Yes, rarely: one thumbnail-sized piece of carrot as an occasional treat. The leafy carrot tops are the better weekly choice.
Yes: a few thumbnail-sized bits of cucumber, skin on, once or twice a week as part of a mixed veg portion.
No. The RSPCA says grapes are poisonous to rodents, and they are sugary too. Never give degus grapes or raisins.
Yes, in small amounts: a few thumbnail-sized pieces of romaine or dark leaf lettuce once or twice a week. Skip iceberg.
Rarely, if at all: one plain, unsalted peanut per degu once a week at most. Never salted, roasted, coated or peanut butter.
Yes, as a tiny reward: one plain, unsalted pumpkin seed per degu, no more than a couple of times a week.
No. Strawberries are too sugary for degus, which are prone to diabetes. A stolen bite is not poisonous, but don't offer them.
Only as a rare reward: one plain, unsalted sunflower seed per degu, a couple of times a week at most. They are very fatty.
Yes, occasionally: a quarter of a ripe cherry tomato per degu. Never the leaves, stalks, vine or unripe green tomatoes.
No: bananas are sugary and starchy, ferrets cannot digest fruit, and the sugar can cause diarrhoea and blood sugar swings.
Only raw meaty bones, with care, and vets disagree even on those. Never give a ferret cooked bones, which can splinter.
Only as a stopgap: most cat food lacks the protein ferrets need, but a high-protein kitten food or a few cat treats will do for a short while.
No: ferrets cope badly with dairy, and cheese is fatty and salty, so it often gives them diarrhoea. Use a meat treat instead.
Yes: plain chicken is one of the best extras for a ferret, given in small pieces alongside a complete ferret food.
No: chocolate is toxic to ferrets and can be fatal. If yours has eaten any, ring a vet straight away.
No: dog food is too starchy and too low in the right protein for ferrets. A few stolen bites will not hurt, but never feed it as a meal.
Yes, as a treat: a little plain cooked egg, or an occasional raw egg in its shell, once or twice a week on top of complete ferret food.
Only now and then: a small piece of plain cooked, boneless fish is not toxic, but meat makes a better treat for a ferret.
No: ferrets are strict meat-eaters that cannot digest fruit, and fruit sugar can cause diarrhoea and blood sugar swings.
No: ferrets should not eat grapes or raisins. They are sugary, hard for ferrets to digest, and grapes can harm the kidneys of other pets.
No: cow's milk often gives ferrets diarrhoea because they cope badly with milk sugar. Clean water is the only drink they need.
No: peanut butter is a fatty, sugary plant food that ferrets cannot digest well, and some brands contain xylitol, which is dangerous to pets.
Yes, ferrets can eat raw meat, but it carries bacteria and blockage risks and must be balanced, so most owners are safer using it as an extra.
Only rarely: a flake of plain tuna in spring water, drained, is not toxic, but fish is not a natural ferret food, so meat treats are better.
Yes, as a treat: a thumbnail-sized piece of apple once or twice a week, with every pip and the core removed.
Yes, as an occasional sweet treat: a quarter of a thin banana slice per gerbil every week or so. No peel, and only plain banana chips.
Yes, as a treat: half a fresh blueberry per gerbil once or twice a week. Dried ones only as a crumb, and never sweetened.
Yes, broccoli is a safe vegetable for gerbils: one small floret, about thumbnail size, per gerbil once or twice a week, raw and washed.
Yes, as a treat: a raw piece of cabbage leaf the size of your thumbnail, around twice a week, with their usual pellets.
Yes, carrot is a safe, crunchy vegetable for gerbils: a thumbnail-sized piece about twice a week, raw and washed.
Yes, as a treat: a raw floret about the size of your thumbnail, around twice a week, alongside their usual pellets.
Yes, occasionally: a thin slice of celery stalk with the strings pulled off. It is watery and low in goodness, so it is never a staple.
No. Cheese is not known to be poisonous, but dairy upsets a gerbil's digestion and is fatty and salty. A stolen crumb is unlikely to harm.
Yes, in small amounts: a quarter of a thin cucumber slice per gerbil once or twice a week. Too much can cause loose droppings.
No. The RSPCA and Burgess say grapes are poisonous to rodents. Never give grapes, raisins, sultanas or currants to a gerbil.
Yes, a small torn leaf of romaine or another dark lettuce once or twice a week. Never iceberg lettuce.
No. Burgess says never feed citrus to gerbils, and Gerbil Care lists oranges, satsumas and lemons as unsafe. Choose apple or berries instead.
Yes, as a treat: about a quarter of a fresh raspberry per gerbil once or twice a week. Skip jam and sweetened dried berries.
Yes, sparingly: one small raw spinach leaf, about the size of your thumbnail, once a week at most.
Yes, as a treat: a thumbnail-sized piece of fresh strawberry per gerbil once or twice a week. The green top is fine too.
Yes, sparingly: a thumbnail-sized piece of ripe red tomato now and then. Never the leaves, stalks or green unripe tomatoes.
Yes, rarely: a thumbnail-sized piece of red watermelon flesh, seeds out. Never the rind, and never a big chunk.
No. Almonds are too fatty and high in calcium for guinea pigs, can cause choking, and bitter almonds are toxic.
Yes, as a treat: a thin slice or two of apple, skin on and pips removed, once or twice a week.
No: avocado flesh, skin, stone and leaves can all harm guinea pigs, and every UK charity lists it as a food to avoid.
Yes, as a small treat: one thin slice of banana, about 1 cm thick, once a week at most. It is one of the most sugary fruits.
Yes, in small amounts: three to five fresh basil leaves a few times a week. It is high in calcium, so not every day.
Yes, as a treat: one or two fresh blueberries per guinea pig, once or twice a week.
No: bread, toast and crusts are starchy and hard for guinea pigs to digest. A crumb is rarely serious, but don't offer it.
Yes, in small amounts: one small raw floret two or three times a week. It is rich in vitamin C, but too much causes gas.
Yes, in small amounts: a palm-sized piece of raw leaf two or three times a week. Savoy and spring greens are good picks; too much causes gas.
Yes, as a treat: a thumb-sized piece of raw carrot two or three times a week. The leafy carrot tops make a better everyday green.
No: cat food is meat-based and very high in protein, which guinea pigs cannot digest. A stolen bite is rarely serious, but watch for 24 hours.
Yes, in small amounts: a floret or a couple of leaves two or three times a week. Too much can cause gas.
Yes: a short piece of celery stalk, chopped small with the strings off, or a few leaves, two or three times a week as part of the veg mix.
No: Cheerios are a starchy, sweetened grain cereal, and vets advise against dry cereals for guinea pigs. One stolen hoop is rarely serious.
No: guinea pigs are plant-eaters that can't digest dairy, and Burgess calls dairy particularly dangerous for them. That includes all cheese, milk and yoghurt.
Yes, as a treat: one fresh cherry, stone and stalk out, about once a week. Never tinned, glacé or cocktail cherries.
No: guinea pigs are strict plant-eaters and cannot digest chicken or any meat. If yours ate some, watch closely and ring your vet.
No, never: chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, which are toxic to pets. If your guinea pig ate any, ring your vet straight away.
Yes: a few sprigs of fresh coriander (cilantro), leaves and stalks, most days of the week as part of the veg bowl.
Yes: a slice or two of raw courgette (zucchini), skin on, is a safe, low-sugar part of the greens mix. The flowers are fine too.
No: crackers are starchy, salty human food that can upset a guinea pig's gut. A stolen nibble is rarely serious.
Yes: a slice or two of washed cucumber, skin and seeds included, can be part of the daily greens mix.
Yes: a few clean, unsprayed dandelion leaves two or three times a week. They are rich in vitamin C but also high in calcium.
No: guinea pigs are strict plant-eaters, and eggs in any form, raw, cooked or shell, are an animal food their gut is not built for.
Yes, as a treat: two seedless grapes, halved, once or twice a week. Skip raisins and seeded grapes.
Yes: fresh, unsprayed grass is ideal, ideally every day. Never feed lawnmower clippings, which ferment and make guinea pigs ill.
Yes, a few times a week: half to one leaf per guinea pig. It is rich in vitamin C but high in calcium, so not every day.
Yes, as a treat: a teaspoon-sized piece of peeled kiwi once a week. It is rich in vitamin C but sugary and acidic.
Yes: romaine (cos), Little Gem and leaf lettuces are good daily greens. Skip iceberg, which is mostly water and can cause loose droppings.
Yes, as a treat: one peeled cube about 2.5 cm (1 in) across, once a week. Mango is very sugary, so keep portions small.
Yes, as a treat: a small cube of melon, skin and seeds off, once or twice a week. Cantaloupe is the best pick.
Yes, now and then: three to five fresh mint leaves once or twice a week. Never mint sauce, sweets or flavoured mint.
No: mushrooms of every kind are on the PDSA and Burgess lists of foods guinea pigs must avoid. Ring your vet if a wild one was eaten.
No: onions and their relatives (spring onions, leeks, shallots, chives, garlic) are toxic to guinea pigs in any form.
Only rarely: a thumb-sized piece of peeled, seedless orange once a week at most. Peppers are a better source of vitamin C.
Yes: two or three sprigs, mixed with other greens, a few times a week. Rich in vitamin C, but high in calcium.
Yes, as a treat: one thin slice of ripe peach, stone removed, once a week. Never give the stone or tinned peaches.
No: peanut butter is high in fat and can stick in a guinea pig's mouth and throat. Nuts and nut spreads have no place in their diet.
No. Peanuts are too fatty for a guinea pig's gut and a choking risk, and shells can carry toxins. Give hay and veg instead.
Yes, as a treat: a thin slice of pear, pips and core out, once or twice a week. The skin is fine once washed.
Yes, a few: five or six fresh peas or a pod or two once or twice a week. The pods and leaves are better than the starchy peas.
Yes: a strip or two of bell pepper a day is one of the best sources of vitamin C for a guinea pig. Never give chilli or hot peppers.
Yes, a little: one small cube of fresh pineapple once a week at most. Skip the skin, core, leaves and tinned pineapple.
No: popcorn is starchy and a choking risk, and salt, butter and toffee make it worse. A dropped piece is rarely serious; a kernel is a choking worry.
No: potatoes and their skin, raw or cooked, are on the charities' lists of foods guinea pigs must not eat.
Yes: a few small cubes of raw pumpkin flesh, a few times a week. No seeds, no skin, nothing cooked, tinned or spiced.
Yes, as a treat: one or two fresh raspberries, once or twice a week. Lower in sugar than most fruit, with useful vitamin C.
No: rice is a starchy grain, and guinea pigs should not eat grains or cooked food. That includes brown rice, uncooked rice and rice cakes.
Yes, in moderation: a few raw leaves two or three times a week. Good vitamin C, but high in calcium and oxalates, so not every day.
Yes, as a treat: one medium strawberry, halved, once or twice a week. One of the best fruits for vitamin C.
No, we'd skip it: a vet-reviewed guide says sweet potato is not safe for guinea pigs, and it is starchy with almost no vitamin C.
A little: a few raw kernels now and then are safe but starchy. The husks and silk are the better part to give a guinea pig.
Yes, the ripe red fruit: one cherry tomato, cut up, once a week. Never the leaves, stalks, vine or green tomatoes.
No. Walnuts are far too fatty for a guinea pig's gut and a choking risk. Give hay, herbs and veg instead.
Yes, as a treat: one 2.5 cm (1 in) cube of watermelon flesh, seeds removed, once or twice a week.
No: Weetabix is a starchy wheat cereal, and vets advise against cereals for guinea pigs. A stolen crumb is rarely serious; Weetabix with milk is worse.
Yes, as a treat: a thumbnail-sized piece of washed apple with the seeds and core removed, once or twice a week. Dwarfs get less.
No: avocado carries persin in its skin, stone and flesh, is very high in fat and can clog cheek pouches, so we never give it to hamsters.
Yes, as a sweet treat: half a thin slice of banana once or twice a week for a Syrian, a crumb now and then for a dwarf. Never banana chips.
No: sweet biscuits (cookies) are too sugary and fatty for hamsters, and chocolate ones are dangerous. Give a hamster treat or a vegetable instead.
Yes, as a treat: about half a blueberry once or twice a week for a Syrian, and a quarter now and then for a dwarf.
Yes: a teaspoon-sized piece of washed pak choi (bok choy) leaf a few times a week is a safe, low-sugar green for Syrian and dwarf hamsters.
Only rarely: a 1 cm piece of dry, plain wholemeal crust now and then. Never raw dough, soft sticky bread, or bread with garlic, seeds or spreads.
Yes: a small floret about the size of your hamster's head, once or twice a week, raw or plainly steamed.
Yes, in small amounts: a small piece of raw leaf no more than twice a week, starting with a nail-sized bit.
Yes: a few small pieces of washed raw carrot, about a quarter teaspoon, a few times a week. Carrot is sweet, so dwarfs have it less often.
No: cat food is far too rich in fat and meat protein for a hamster. A stolen piece of kibble is not an emergency, but do not feed it.
Yes: a small piece of raw floret, about 1 cm (0.4 in) across, once or twice a week. Leave out the leaves and tough stem.
Yes, with the strings removed: about half a teaspoon of finely chopped celery once or twice a week.
Best not: Burgess and Omlet both say to avoid dairy for hamsters. A stolen crumb is not an emergency, but boiled egg is a better protein treat.
Yes, rarely: a quarter of a fresh cherry with the stone, stalk and leaves removed, every 7 to 10 days for a Syrian. Dwarfs get a crumb or none.
Yes, cooked and plain: half a chickpea once or twice a week for a Syrian, a quarter for a dwarf. Never raw, salted, roasted or as hummus.
No: chips (fries) and crisps are salty, oily, often seasoned and made from potato, which charities list as unsafe for hamsters.
No: chocolate of any kind is dangerous to hamsters. If yours has eaten some, ring your vet straight away, even if they seem fine.
Yes: a washed cube of raw courgette (zucchini) about 1 cm (0.4 in) across, two or three times a week. Low in sugar, so fine for dwarfs.
Only rarely: a 1 cm piece of a plain, unsalted wholegrain cracker now and then. Salted, cheesy and flavoured crackers are a no.
Yes: one or two dried pet-shop crickets once or twice a week make a natural protein treat. Skip live crickets, and never feed wild-caught insects.
Yes: a thin slice of washed cucumber once or twice a week is a safe, low-sugar treat for Syrian and dwarf hamsters alike.
Best not: dates are dried fruit packed with sugar, so we skip them for all hamsters and give a fresh fruit or vegetable treat instead.
No: dog food has too much fat and protein and too little fibre for a hamster. A stolen piece is fine, but do not feed it on purpose.
Yes: a fingernail-sized piece of plain hard-boiled or scrambled egg once or twice a week is a good protein treat. Never raw, runny or seasoned.
Best not: the RSPCA says never to give hamsters grapes, as they can be poisonous to rodents, so pick a safer fruit such as apple or blueberry.
Yes, as a rare treat: a quarter of a plain, unsalted hazelnut once a week for a Syrian, and a crumb for a dwarf. Never chocolate hazelnut spread.
Yes, in moderation: a head-sized piece of soft leaf once or twice a week for an adult Syrian, with no stem and none for babies.
Yes, as a treat: a paw-sized piece of ripe, peeled kiwi about once a week for a Syrian, and only a crumb for dwarf hamsters.
Yes, in small amounts: a teaspoon-sized piece of washed romaine or other dark lettuce once or twice a week. Skip iceberg, which is mostly water.
Yes, as a rare treat for Syrians: a 1 cm cube of fresh, peeled mango every week or two. Skip it for Campbell's, winter white and Chinese hamsters.
Yes, for Syrians: about a teaspoon of fresh melon flesh, no rind or seeds, once or twice a week. Skip it for dwarf and baby hamsters.
Rarely: a fingernail-sized piece of plain, shop-bought mushroom now and then. Never wild mushrooms, and nothing cooked in butter, oil or garlic.
Some, as a rare treat: one small piece of a plain, unsalted nut such as walnut or hazelnut, once a week at most. Never salted or flavoured nuts.
No: onions and their relatives (garlic, leeks, chives, spring onions) can damage red blood cells, so never feed them to a hamster, raw or cooked.
No: oranges and other citrus are too acidic and sugary for hamsters, and UK charities advise leaving them out. A bite is not poisonous.
Yes: a paw-sized piece of fresh, washed peach about once a week for a Syrian, never the stone. Dwarf hamsters are better off skipping it.
No: peanut butter is sticky enough to clog cheek pouches and is high in fat, salt and sugar. A plain unsalted peanut now and then is the safer swap.
Yes, plain and unsalted: one peanut once or twice a week for a Syrian, a quarter for a dwarf. Never salted, honey-roasted or chocolate peanuts.
Yes: a thin slice of washed pear the size of your hamster's ear, pips and core removed, about once a week. Dwarfs get less, less often.
Yes for Syrians: up to six plain peas a week, two at a time at most. Robos up to three a week. Campbell's and winter whites are better without.
Yes for sweet bell peppers: a small strip two or three times a week. Chillies and any hot or spicy pepper are a no.
Yes, rarely: a 1 cm cube of fresh pineapple flesh once every two weeks for a Syrian. No skin, core, tinned fruit or juice, and skip it for dwarfs.
Yes, if plain and unsalted: half a shelled pistachio once a week for a Syrian, a crumb for a dwarf. Never salted or flavoured ones.
Yes, plain only: one or two pieces of air-popped popcorn now and then. No butter, salt, sugar, toffee or microwave popcorn.
No: raw and green potato contains solanine, and UK sources list potato as unsafe for hamsters. Chips and crisps are a no too.
Yes: plain pumpkin flesh, raw or cooked, in a piece the size of your hamster's ear a few times a week, plus the odd plain pumpkin seed.
Yes, as a treat: a piece about the size of your hamster's head, no more than once a week, and less for a dwarf.
Yes, plain rice is safe: a few dry grains, or a pinch of plain cooked rice, now and then. Never fried, salted, seasoned or sticky rice.
Yes: one or two washed baby spinach leaves, two or three times a week, rotated with other greens.
Yes for Syrians: a fingernail-sized piece once or twice a week. Dwarf hamsters are best skipping strawberries because of the sugar.
Yes: a peeled, plain piece of sweet potato the size of your fingernail, raw or cooked, once or twice a week.
Yes for Syrians and Roborovskis: one or two plain kernels a couple of times a week. Campbell's and winter white dwarfs should skip it.
Best not: Woodgreen lists tomato as harmful, and the leaves, stalks and green fruit are poisonous to hamsters. Offer cucumber or pepper instead.
Yes, now and then: a seedless cube of red flesh about 1 cm (0.4 in) across, once a week at most.
Only a dry crumb now and then: a fingernail-sized piece of plain Weetabix is fine for a Syrian. Never with milk, and skip flavoured kinds.
Yes, as a treat: a fingernail-sized piece of apple once or twice a week, with every pip, the core and the stalk removed.
Yes, as an occasional treat: a fingernail-sized piece of ripe banana, about once a week. It is very sugary, so keep it small.
Yes, as a treat: about half a blueberry per mouse, once or twice a week. Fresh or frozen and thawed, never dried, sweetened or in muffins.
Yes, broccoli is an everyday vegetable for mice: a fingernail-sized piece of washed floret per mouse, raw or plainly steamed.
Yes, a little: a thumbnail-sized piece of raw green cabbage leaf two or three times a week. Darker savoy and spring greens are the best types.
Yes: carrot is a good mouse vegetable. A thin slice (about 0.5 g) a few times a week, raw and washed, rotated with greens.
Yes, as an extra: a fingernail-sized piece of raw cauliflower two or three times a week. Darker greens like broccoli and kale are better daily.
Only now and then. Celery is not harmful, but it is mostly water: a tiny string-free piece of stalk or a celery leaf, occasionally, is the most to give.
Best not: cheese is not poisonous, but adult mice digest dairy poorly and it is fatty and salty, so skip it and offer a pea-sized piece of veg instead.
No: chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, which are toxic to mice even in small amounts. Dark chocolate and cocoa powder are the most dangerous.
Yes, a crumb of plain or wholegrain cracker once or twice a week is fine. Skip salted, cheesy, buttery or flavoured crackers.
Yes: a thin, fingernail-sized piece of cucumber, peeled or unpeeled, a few times a week. It is mostly water, so pair it with greens.
No: the RSPCA and RSPCA Australia both say not to feed grapes or raisins to mice. Ring a vet if your mouse has eaten some.
Yes, kale is an everyday green for mice: a small torn piece of washed leaf, about the size of a thumbnail, per mouse, stem removed.
No: PetMD says mice should not eat citrus, and lemon is the most acidic. A lick won't poison a mouse, but don't offer it.
No. The RSPCA says not to feed pet mice lettuce because it can cause diarrhoea. Kale, broccoli and pak choi are better greens.
Best not: PetMD says mice should not eat citrus, so skip oranges, satsumas and juice. A nibble is unlikely to cause more than a mild upset.
Yes, as a treat: a small piece of raspberry, about a quarter of one berry per mouse, once or twice a week. Fresh or thawed, never jam or sweetened.
Yes, now and then: a thumbnail-sized piece of raw spinach leaf once or twice a week. It is high in oxalates, so kale makes a better daily green.
Yes, as a treat: a fingernail-sized piece of strawberry (0.5 to 1 g) once or twice a week. Wash it and take off the green top.
Yes, ripe tomato flesh in a fingernail-sized piece once a week. Never unripe tomatoes, leaves, stalks or the plant.
Yes, as a treat: a fingernail-sized cube of red watermelon flesh, seeds out, once or twice a week. Skip the rind.
No. Orange peel isn't poisonous, but it is tough, oily and may carry pesticide, so peel any orange before a rabbit gets a bite.
Yes, as a treat: a thin slice (about an eighth of an apple), pips and core removed, once or twice a week.
No. Avocado is on the avoid lists of the RSPCA, Burgess and Woodgreen: it is very fatty, and the plant is known to harm some animals.
Yes, rarely: one thin slice of peeled banana, about once a week. It is one of the sweetest fruits a rabbit can have.
No. Human biscuits (cookies) are sugar, fat and flour. Rabbit nuggets, sometimes called rabbit biscuits, are fine in measured amounts.
Yes, as a treat: two or three fresh blueberries, once or twice a week, for an average rabbit.
Yes. Bok choy (pak choi) is a safe leafy green: feed it raw, leaves and stalks, as one of several greens in the daily mix.
No. Bread is starchy and low in fibre, and the RSPCA lists it among foods to avoid. A stolen crust is rarely an emergency, but watch the droppings.
Yes, in moderation: a small raw floret or some leaves a few times a week. The leaves are the best part; too much can cause gas.
No: buckwheat groats, flakes and flour are starchy seeds, and rabbit charities advise against grains and cereals. Stick to hay and greens.
Yes: a leaf or two of raw cabbage a few times a week, rotated with other greens. Too much at once can cause gas.
Yes, as a treat only: a piece about 1 cm across, once or twice a week. Carrots are sugary; the leafy tops are the better daily green.
No. Cat food is meat-based and low in fibre. Remove it, watch appetite and droppings, and ring a vet if either drops.
Yes, in moderation. The leaves are the best part, florets are fine in small pieces. Rotate it with other greens as brassicas can cause gas.
Yes: raw celery leaves and a short piece of stalk, cut small, a few times a week. Too much every day is not ideal.
No. Cheese is fatty dairy with no fibre, and the RSPCA lists dairy among foods rabbits must avoid. Remove it and watch appetite and droppings.
Yes, as a treat: one fresh cherry (two for a big rabbit), stone and stalk removed, once a week. Never the stones, leaves or glace cherries.
No. Chocolate is toxic to rabbits. If yours ate any, ring your vet straight away with the type and amount, without waiting for signs.
Yes: a slice or two of raw courgette (zucchini) a few times a week. The flowers are fine too; skip the leaves.
No: crackers are starchy, salty and low in fibre, and rabbit charities list them as foods to avoid. One stolen bite is rarely an emergency.
Yes, as an extra: one or two thin slices of raw cucumber a few times a week. Cucumber leaves are safe too.
No. Rabbits are strict plant-eaters, and the RSPCA lists eggs alongside meat and dairy as foods rabbits should avoid, cooked or raw.
Yes: fennel fronds, stalks and bulb are all safe raw, as one of the greens in a daily mix. Leave out fennel seeds.
Yes, as a rare treat: one grape, halved, once or twice a week at most. No raisins, juice or grape leaves from sprayed vines.
Yes, in moderation: a leaf or two, raw, a few times a week. Kale is high in calcium and a gassy brassica, so rotate it with other greens.
Yes, as a treat: one thin slice of peeled kiwi fruit, about 5 mm (1/4 in) thick, once a week.
No. Leeks are in the onion family and the RSPCA lists them as a food to avoid. If your rabbit ate some, ring your vet.
Yes, dark lettuce such as romaine is a good daily green, mixed with others. Iceberg is a no: watery, low in goodness and linked to loose droppings.
Yes, as a rare treat: one peeled cube about 2 cm (3/4 in) across, once a week. Never the stone, and skip dried mango.
No: the RSPCA lists mushrooms as a food to avoid, and wild garden fungi can be poisonous. Ring your vet if your rabbit has eaten a wild one.
No. Onions and the rest of the onion family, cooked or raw, are on the avoid lists of the RSPCA and Rabbit Welfare Association.
Only rarely: a quarter of a peeled segment, pips out, once or twice a month for an adult rabbit. No peel or juice.
Yes. Pak choi is an RWAF-listed leafy green: serve it raw, leaves and stalks, as one of five or six fresh foods in the day.
Yes, as a treat: a small piece of raw parsnip, about 1 cm across, once or twice a week. Never cooked or roasted.
Yes, as a treat: one thin slice of fresh peach, stone removed, once a week. Never the stone or leaves, and no tinned peaches.
No. Peanut butter is very high in fat, nuts and legumes are on rabbit avoid lists, and some brands contain xylitol. Never use it as a treat.
Yes, as a treat: up to an eighth of a pear, with the core and pips cut out, once or twice a week. Pear leaves and twigs are fine too.
Flat pods yes: one or two sugar snap or mangetout pods a few times a week. Shelled, frozen or tinned peas are too starchy, so skip them.
Yes, sweet bell peppers in small pieces, seeds and stalk removed, once or twice a week. Green is lowest in sugar. Chilli peppers are a no.
Yes, as a treat: one small chunk of fresh, peeled pineapple about 2 cm (3/4 in) across, once a week. No skin, crown or tinned pineapple.
